answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt failed on a platform modernization delivery.

Matt was the tech lead for a global financial services engagement with development, QA, UAT, and production environments. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from prior phases, along with documentation.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. He relied on that documentation instead of verifying it. He assumed access controls and environment boundaries were correct, did not audit who could trigger downstream email jobs, and did not verify that production customer names and email addresses had been masked or scrubbed. Data masking and email interception were not in place as compensating controls.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments.

The client demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence,” and said leaders own the environment their teams operate in.

Afterward, Matt made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one leadership responsibilities in his delivery approach. His wording for the lesson was: “assumptions are risks in disguise.”
